name: Isaiah
v: Comfort. Comfort my people — this is what your God is saying.
Speak straight to Jerusalem's heart. Tell her the hard service is finished, the debt is settled, that she has taken from the LORD's hand double for every wrong.
A voice is calling out: Clear a road for the LORD through the wilderness. Cut a straight highway across the wasteland for our God.
Every valley — fill it in. Every mountain and hill — bring it down. The crooked places, make them straight. The rough country, smooth it out.
Then the glory of the LORD will be unveiled, and every human being alive will see it together. The mouth of the LORD has spoken.
A voice says: Call out. And I said: What should I call? — All flesh is grass, and every kindness of it like the wildflower in the field.
The grass withers, the flower fades, when the breath of the LORD blows across it. Yes — the people are grass.
The grass withers. The flower fades. But the word of our God stands forever.

Climb a high mountain, you who carry good news to Zion. Lift your voice with everything in you, you who carry good news to Jerusalem. Lift it — don't be afraid. Tell the cities of Judah: Here is your God.
Look — the Lord GOD is coming in strength, and his arm rules for him. His reward travels with him; what he has won walks ahead of him.
He will tend his flock the way a shepherd does — gathering lambs into the crook of his arm, carrying them against his chest, leading the nursing ewes with care.

Who has measured the oceans in the cup of his hand? Who marked off the sky with the span of his fingers? Who held the dust of the earth in a bucket, weighed the mountains on a scale, the hills in a balance?
Who has charted the Spirit of the LORD, or stood at his elbow giving counsel?
Whom did he consult? Who taught him? Who showed him the path of justice, schooled him in knowledge, walked him through the way of understanding?
Look — the nations are a drop falling from a bucket. They count as dust on the scales. He lifts whole islands like grains of sand.
All Lebanon could not fuel his fire. All its beasts could not be sacrifice enough.
Every nation, set before him, is nothing. Less than nothing. Empty.
So who will you compare to God? What image will you set beside him?
An idol? A craftsman pours it. A goldsmith plates it. He fits it with silver chains.
Too poor for that? Then someone picks out wood that won't rot, finds a skilled carver, and sets up an idol that will not move.
Do you not know this? Have you not heard? Was it not told to you from the beginning? Have you not understood since the foundations of the earth were laid?
He sits enthroned above the circle of the earth, and the people on it look like grasshoppers. He stretches out the heavens like fabric, spreads them like a tent to live under.
He reduces rulers to nothing. He makes the judges of the earth meaningless.
Barely planted, barely sown, barely rooted in the ground — he blows on them, and they wither. The whirlwind carries them off like straw.
So to whom will you compare me? Who is my equal? — says the Holy One.
Lift your eyes. Look up. Who created all these? He brings out their armies by number; he calls each one by name. Because his power is overwhelming, his strength absolute, not one of them is missing.
So why are you saying, Jacob — why claim, Israel — My road is hidden from the LORD; my God has lost track of my cause?
Have you not known? Have you not heard? The LORD is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He does not grow tired. He does not grow weary. His understanding has no bottom.
He gives strength to the exhausted. To those with nothing left, he multiplies power.
Even the young grow tired and stumble. Even the strong fall flat.
But those who wait on the LORD will find their strength renewed. They will rise on wings like eagles. They will run and not collapse. They will walk and not give out.

com.d:
# Isaiah 40: The Comfort of God's Eternal Greatness

The spiritual heart of Isaiah 40 is this: when our strength fails and our vision dims, God's Word stands forever, and His tender compassion meets us in our exhaustion. The prophet opens with a sweeping declaration of comfort that echoes across centuries to reach us in our weariness—"Comfort, comfort my people," the Lord says, inviting us into a relationship where our deepest struggles are met not with dismissal but with divine tenderness.

What makes this comfort authentic is that it emerges not from denying our pain but from positioning it against the backdrop of God's incomparable greatness. Isaiah invites us to lift our eyes to the heavens and ask: "Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand? Who has marked off the heavens with the span of a hand?" These rhetorical questions aren't meant to overwhelm us with divine distance but to anchor us in the truth that the One who holds creation itself also holds our sorrows. A God this mighty, Isaiah insists, is utterly trustworthy with our weakness.

The passage captures something profoundly human: we grow weary. Our strength fails like grass that withers and flowers that fade. Perhaps you're carrying burdens that have exhausted your reserves—relational heartbreak, physical illness, spiritual confusion, vocational discouragement. The ancient world knew this weariness, and so does ours. Isaiah doesn't offer denial or minimization. Instead, he points us to the One whose strength never diminishes and whose understanding is beyond measure.

Yet the most stirring promise comes near the passage's end: "Those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength." Not escape their circumstances, but renew their strength. Not bypass difficulty, but find resilience within it. The God who commands the stars also mounts us on eagle's wings.

What area of your life feels most exhausted right now? Can you bring that weariness before the God whose love outlasts the cosmos, asking Him to renew not just your strength, but your trust in His eternal care?
com.s:
Isaiah 40 marks a dramatic theological and literary transition within the book, opening what scholars commonly designate as "Deutero-Isaiah" or the "Book of Comfort" (chapters 40–55). Whether composed by the eighth-century prophet himself with prophetic foresight or by a later exilic author writing in Isaiah's tradition, this chapter addresses a community experiencing or anticipating Babylonian exile, offering profound consolation through declarations of divine sovereignty and redemptive purpose.

The chapter commences with the imperative "comfort" (*naḥamu*, נַחֲמוּ), repeated for emphasis in the Hebrew, establishing the pastoral tone that pervades this section. This verbal form, a piel imperative plural, suggests intensive action directed toward the covenant community, signaling a decisive shift from the judgments characterizing earlier chapters. The divine council imagery in verses 1–8 echoes ancient Near Eastern throne-room scenes, with heavenly voices proclaiming preparation for Yahweh's advent—imagery later applied to John the Baptist in the Gospel traditions.

Central to the chapter's theology is the term *dāḇār* (דָּבָר), "word," which in verse 8 stands eternally against transient human existence compared to withering grass. This theological affirmation grounds Israel's hope not in political circumstances but in divine speech-acts that accomplish their purposes. The contrast between fading flora and enduring divine word employs imagery deeply resonant within Palestinian agricultural experience.

The latter portion introduces the incomparability motif through rhetorical questions challenging any adequate comparison to Yahweh. The term *ʾēl* (אֵל) appears alongside *Elohim*, emphasizing divine power against the backdrop of Babylonian religious claims. Verses 12–26 systematically dismantle confidence in created things, imperial powers, and manufactured deities, while verses 27–31 address Israel's complaint of divine neglect.

The chapter culminates with the celebrated promise that those waiting upon Yahweh will renew strength, mounting with wings like eagles. The verb *qāwâ* (קָוָה), "to wait," connotes expectant hope and active trust rather than passive resignation. This theological vocabulary shaped subsequent Jewish and Christian spirituality profoundly.

Interpreters debate whether this chapter functioned as prophetic prediction, exilic proclamation, or liturgical composition for temple restoration. Regardless of compositional setting, Isaiah 40 remains a masterwork of Hebrew poetry addressing perennial questions of divine presence amid historical suffering.
com.p:
Isaiah 40 stands at a pivotal juncture in prophetic history, written approximately 700 years before the incarnation of Christ during the latter years of the eighth century BC. Though the prophet ministered during the reigns of Uzziah through Hezekiah, the Spirit here carries his vision far beyond his own era—past the Babylonian exile that would not occur for another century, into the dawn of messianic redemption, and ultimately to the consummation of all things. Within the grand arc of redemptive history, this chapter serves as a prophetic bridge between the coming exile and the promised restoration, yet its deepest fulfillment transcends Israel's return from Babylon to announce the greater exodus accomplished in Christ.

The opening words, "Comfort, comfort my people," mark a dramatic shift from the preceding chapters of judgment. Heaven's council speaks, declaring that Jerusalem's warfare is ended and her iniquity pardoned. This comfort finds its historical echo in Cyrus's decree permitting Israel's return, yet the doubling of "comfort" signals a deeper redemption—the double portion of grace that would come through Messiah's atoning work.

The voice crying in the wilderness to prepare the way of the Lord constitutes one of Scripture's most explicit prophetic fulfillments. All four Gospels identify John the Baptist as this forerunner, making the highway straight for Israel's God who would walk among His people in human flesh. What Isaiah glimpsed across seven centuries materialized when the eternal Word tabernacled in creation, and John stood at Jordan's banks announcing the Lamb who takes away the world's sin.

The typological richness deepens as the chapter unfolds. The shepherd who gathers lambs in his arms and gently leads nursing ewes prefigures Christ the Good Shepherd, who lays down his life for the sheep. The imagery of grass withering and flowers fading while God's word stands forever finds its ultimate expression in the incarnate Word who remains the same yesterday, today, and forever.

Yet eschatological threads extend beyond the first advent. The arm of the Lord revealed, the glory of the Lord displayed for all flesh to see together, and the coming with might to render recompense—these await final fulfillment when Christ returns in power. The rhetorical questions concerning God's incomparability, His measuring of waters and weighing of mountains, remind the church that the One who orchestrates history remains sovereign over every nation and ruler until He makes all enemies a footstool.

For believers dwelling between the advents, Isaiah 40 speaks comfort still: the same God who pardons sin, who strengthens the weary, and who causes those who wait upon Him to mount up with wings as eagles remains faithful to complete what He began.
